newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Southern Belgian magistrates stage protest strikes.
newsitem.headline: Southern Belgian magistrates stage protest strikes.

text.p: Magistrates from Brussels and the Francophone south of Belgium staged symbolic strikes on Tuesday in protest at accusations of incompetence in the country's child kidnapping, abuse and murder scandals.

Their anger has erupted into a war of words between the magistrates and politicians, particularly Dutch-speaking Justice Minister Stefaan De Clerck, that threatens to sour efforts to reform Belgium's antiquated judicial and police system.

The magistrates, who complain of being swamped with cases, stopped work at 10.30 a.m. to demonstrate against an official report accusing them of sloth and a lack of professionalism in their handling of the child disappearances.
It was the first strike by the magistrates since 1989, but their complaints were largely the same.
"We are trying to draw to the attention of all the authorities...that these problems cannot be solved from one day to the next," Brussels Public Prosecutor Benoit Dejemeppe told RTBF television.

The report, approved unanimously by parliament two weeks ago, said at least two of the five young girls found dead since last August might have been rescued if police and magistrates had spent more time working with rather than against each other.
In particular it accused Dejemeppe of being incapable, prompting De Clerck to ask him to resign or at least step aside.

But Dejemeppe, supported by his staff, has refused to go, and the magistrates -- overworked and under-resourced -- have threatened to reopen the hundreds of dormant missing persons files they have been unable to tackle due to lack of personnel.
"In general we lack staff," Mons Public Prosecutor Pierre Honore said.

The magistrates accuse De Clerck of having for years ignored their pleas for more resources, and in Brussels of contributing to the problem by insisting that any new appointments be fluent in both French and Dutch -- the two languages of the city.
The fight prompted one member of the parliamentary commission which conducted the report to lash out.

"If the magistrates had been as energetic in their efforts to find the children as they are in defending themselves, we wouldn't be here," Flemish Socialist Party member Renaat Landuyt said at the weekend.
The commission report, which followed six months of hearings that riveted the nation, spared no one in its description of the shambolic investigations into the child kidnappings.
Police have found the bodies of eight-year-olds Julie Lejeune, Melissa Russo and Loubna Benaissa as well as those of teenagers An Marchal and Eefje Lambrecks, and they are still looking for more.
The bodies have all been found either in the south of Belgium or in Brussels.
Two convicted child rapists -- Marc Dutroux and Patrick Derochette -- have been charged with murder.
The all-party report made recommendations ranging from creation of a single police force to replace the existing three rival forces, to reform of the whole justice system.

The commission will continue its work until the end of September to try to give substance to its theory that Dutroux and Derochette and their accomplices might have escaped arrest earlier because they had high level protection.
